newsitem.title: USA: Andrew Lloyd Webber says time for a curtain call.
newsitem.headline: Andrew Lloyd Webber says time for a curtain call.

text.p: Britain's Andrew Lloyd Webber, who has dazzled theatre audiences for two decades and who opens "Whistle Down the Wind" this week, said on Monday it might now be time for a breather in his career.
"This is the first time I can truthfully say that I don't have an idea for a show at all," Lloyd Webber told a luncheon at the National Press Club.

In wide-ranging and often humorous remarks that touched on music, architecture, art and critics, the creator of mega-hits like "Cats," "Phantom of the Opera," "Evita," and "Sunset Boulevard" said the only thing he had in mind right now was writing a book about his art collection.
"At this point, I've written more musicals than Rodgers and Hammerstein did when they were together," he said. "Perhaps it's time to take stock of things and recharge the batteries."

The only other distant project he said he had in mind was to rework "Aspects of Love," a little known play of his that was not a commercial success but which he said was a favourite. He said he might get back to it after the art book was done.
Lloyd Webber spoke to the media before his Cajun-flavored, rock and gospel "Whistle Down the Wind" opens to previews on Friday at the National Threatre, a few blocks from the White House.

An American story based in Louisiana, it will be the first world opening of one of his shows outside England since "Jesus Christ Superstar" -- "a horrible glitzy production on Broadway I couldn't stand," he said -- opened in 1971.

This version of "Whistle," set in Louisiana in 1959, may be American, but it is based on a 1960s-era novel and movie set in the north of England in which three children shelter a stranger in their barn, believing he is Jesus Christ. The Louisiana bayou setting allowed Lloyd Webber to draw on the musical influences of gospel and early rock 'n' roll.
The piece is smaller in scale and features spoken diologue, a change from the lavish musical productions that brought Lloyd Webber fame and fortune.

"I have been quoted as saying the era of mega-musicals is ending, but that is not exactly what I said." He explained the era has big threater has become too expensive while ticket prices have risen about as high as they could.

As threater has changed, he also lamented the lack of new writers with whom he could interact. "It would be wonderful to see a whole lot of new people come along," he said. "You don't have anyone to bounce off."
Lloyd Webber, who has often kept a low profile with the media and has at times received a harsh reception at critics' hands, didn't display any bitterness when the subject came up at the luncheon.
He pointed out that many of his works have been well received but he accepted that some critics would never like his productions.
"Some people don't like my stuff but that's completely understandable," said the man who once named a race horse after a New York Times critic.
